selectiveHotelling: selective inference for clustering with an unknown covariance Yiqun T. Chen and Lucy L. Gao 2026-10-07 Overview Clustering is often followed by a test of whether two of the estimated clusters have different means. If the same data are used both to form the clusters and to test them, a classical two-sample test, such as Hotelling’s \(T^2\) test, rejects true null hypotheses far more often than its nominal level: the clustering algorithm has already chosen groups that look different. selectiveHotelling computes selective \(p\)-values, which account for the fact that the clusters were estimated from the data. A test based on these \(p\)-values rejects a true null hypothesis with probability at most \(\alpha\) among the data sets on which the clustering returns the tested clusters. Unlike earlier selective tests for clustering, the tests in this package do not need the covariance matrix of the features: it can be unknown and unstructured. The tests work with any clustering algorithm. This tutorial covers \(k\)-means clustering (Chapter 1), hierarchical clustering (Chapter 2), any other clustering algorithm (Chapter 3), a faster one-dimensional test (Chapter 4), a real data example (Chapter 5), and the ideas behind the tests and practical advice (Chapter 6). Installation # install.packages("remotes") remotes::install_github("yiqunchen/selectiveHotelling") The package depends only on base R. This tutorial also uses the palmerpenguins data in Chapter 5. Citation If you use the package, please cite Chen, Y. T. and Gao, L. L. Selective inference for clustering under unknown covariance. The code that reproduces the paper is at https://github.com/yiqunchen/selectiveHotelling-paper.

Chapter 1 Tutorial: \(k\)-means clustering 1.1 Simulated data 1.2 Cluster and test 1.3 Compare with the naive test 1.4 Data with no groups 1.5 Repeating the experiment 1.6 Fixing the \(k\)-means initialization

Chapter 1 Tutorial: \(k\)-means clustering library(selectiveHotelling) 1.1 Simulated data We generate \(n = 150\) observations in \(p = 2\) dimensions from three groups of \(50\), whose means differ by \(6\) along the first feature. The two features are correlated, and the analysis below never uses their covariance matrix. set.seed(123) n_per <- 50 Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1), 2, 2) noise <- matrix(rnorm(3 * n_per * 2), ncol = 2) %*% chol(Sigma) mu <- rbind(c(-6, 0), c(0, 0), c(6, 0))[rep(1:3, each = n_per), ] X <- mu + noise true_group <- rep(1:3, each = n_per) 1.2 Cluster and test selective_hotelling_test() runs \(k\)-means with \(K\) clusters and tests the null hypothesis that clusters k1 and k2 share one mean. It returns the selective \(p\)-value and the clustering that was tested. set.seed(1) # fixes the random initial centers of k-means res12 <- selective_hotelling_test(X, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, K = 3, M = 1000) res12 #> Selective Hotelling T^2 test (unknown covariance) #> Clusters tested : 1 vs 2 (of K = 3) #> Sampler : besag-clifford #> Conditioning : pair-preserved #> Observed T^2 : 1195 #> Selective p-val : 0.004965 (MC s.e. ~ 0.002) The default path length is M = 5000; we use M = 1000 in this tutorial so that it runs quickly. Chapter 6 explains this choice. The estimated clusters agree with the true groups: table(cluster = res12$cluster, true_group) #> true_group #> cluster 1 2 3 #> 1 0 50 0 #> 2 0 0 50 #> 3 50 0 0 plot(X, col = res12$cluster, pch = 19, xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2", main = "") 1.3 Compare with the naive test The naive test applies Hotelling’s \(T^2\) test to the estimated clusters as if they had been chosen in advance. We compute it for every pair of clusters, next to the selective test. naive_pval <- function(X, cl, k1, k2) { n1 <- sum(cl == k1); n2 <- sum(cl == k2); p <- ncol(X); r <- n1 + n2 F_stat <- (r - p - 1) / ((r - 2) * p) * hotelling_T2(X, cl, k1, k2) pf(F_stat, p, r - p - 1, lower.tail = FALSE) } pairs <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(1, 3), c(2, 3)) results <- t(apply(pairs, 1, function(k) { set.seed(1) # the same initial centers, so the same clustering, for every pair sel <- selective_hotelling_test(X, k[1], k[2], K = 3, M = 1000) c(k1 = k[1], k2 = k[2], naive = naive_pval(X, sel$cluster, k[1], k[2]), selective = sel$pval) })) signif(results, 3) #> k1 k2 naive selective #> [1,] 1 2 4.64e-55 0.00497 #> [2,] 1 3 8.41e-60 0.00596 #> [3,] 2 3 1.24e-84 0.00397 Both tests reject every null hypothesis here, because the three groups really differ. The difference between the tests appears when there are no groups at all. 1.4 Data with no groups Now all \(n = 150\) observations come from one Gaussian distribution, so every null hypothesis is true. set.seed(321) X0 <- matrix(rnorm(150 * 2), ncol = 2) %*% chol(Sigma) res0 <- selective_hotelling_test(X0, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, K = 3, M = 1000) c(naive = naive_pval(X0, res0$cluster, 1, 2), selective = res0$pval) #> naive selective #> 2.023292e-26 3.001798e-01 The naive \(p\)-value is tiny, although the clusters are only an artifact of \(k\)-means. The selective \(p\)-value is not. 1.5 Repeating the experiment To see that this is not a coincidence, we repeat the null experiment \(300\) times with \(n = 60\) and plot the quantiles of the \(p\)-values against those of the uniform distribution. We skip the rare data sets in which a tested cluster has fewer than three observations, for which Hotelling’s \(T^2\) is not defined. A test that controls the Type I error has \(p\)-values on or above the diagonal. set.seed(2024) sim <- t(replicate(300, { Xs <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 2), ncol = 2) %*% chol(Sigma) rs <- tryCatch(selective_hotelling_test(Xs, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, K = 3, M = 200), error = function(e) NULL) # skip the rare data sets with a tiny cluster if (is.null(rs)) c(naive = NA, selective = NA) else c(naive = naive_pval(Xs, rs$cluster, 1, 2), selective = rs$pval) })) sim <- sim[complete.cases(sim), ] nrow(sim) #> [1] 299 u <- ppoints(nrow(sim)) plot(u, sort(sim[, "naive"]), pch = 19, col = "black", xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Uniform(0, 1) quantiles", ylab = "p-value quantiles") points(u, sort(sim[, "selective"]), pch = 19, col = "steelblue") abline(0, 1, lty = 2) legend("topleft", c("naive", "selective"), col = c("black", "steelblue"), pch = 19, bty = "n") colMeans(sim <= 0.05) #> naive selective #> 1.0000000 0.0735786 At level \(0.05\), the naive test rejects 100% of these true null hypotheses and the selective test 7.4%. With about \(300\) data sets, the second number has a Monte Carlo standard error of about \(1.3\) percentage points; in a run with \(2{,}000\) data sets, the selective test rejected \(4.7\%\). 1.6 Fixing the \(k\)-means initialization \(k\)-means depends on its random initial centers. selective_hotelling_test() draws the initial centers once, from the current random seed, and reruns \(k\)-means from the same centers inside the test; set a seed before calling it to make the result reproducible. To choose the initial centers yourself, pass a clustering function to selective_hotelling_bc(), as in Chapter 3: init <- c(1, 51, 101) # rows used as initial centers cl_fun <- function(x) kmeans_with_fixed_init(x, init_centers_idx = init)$cluster selective_hotelling_bc(X, cl_fun, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, M = 1000)$pval #> [1] 0.006090536

Chapter 2 Tutorial: hierarchical clustering

Chapter 2 Tutorial: hierarchical clustering library(selectiveHotelling) For hierarchical clustering, set clustering = "hclust". By default the package uses average linkage on squared Euclidean distances and cuts the tree into K clusters; hclust_method chooses another linkage. set.seed(123) Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1), 2, 2) X <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2), matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2) + 4) %*% chol(Sigma) res <- selective_hotelling_test(X, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, K = 2, clustering = "hclust", M = 1000) res #> Selective Hotelling T^2 test (unknown covariance) #> Clusters tested : 1 vs 2 (of K = 2) #> Sampler : besag-clifford #> Conditioning : pair-preserved #> Observed T^2 : 842.1 #> Selective p-val : 0.002837 (MC s.e. ~ 0.002) table(res$cluster) #> #> 1 2 #> 50 50 The two clusters come from two different groups, and the test rejects. With a single group, it does not: set.seed(321) X0 <- matrix(rnorm(200), ncol = 2) %*% chol(Sigma) res0 <- selective_hotelling_test(X0, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, K = 2, clustering = "hclust", M = 1000) res0$pval #> [1] 0.4715096 With complete linkage: selective_hotelling_test(X, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, K = 2, clustering = "hclust", hclust_method = "complete", M = 1000)$pval #> [1] 0.0002489197 Average-linkage hierarchical clustering is sensitive to outliers. Chapter 6 discusses when the tests rely on Gaussian data.

Chapter 3 Tutorial: any clustering algorithm 3.1 Partitioning around medoids 3.2 A clustering function with a random step 3.3 What selective_hotelling_bc() returns

Chapter 3 Tutorial: any clustering algorithm library(selectiveHotelling) The test needs only one thing from the clustering algorithm: a function cl_fun that takes a data matrix and returns a vector of cluster labels. selective_hotelling_bc() reruns this function on perturbed versions of the data and keeps the perturbations under which the tested clusters are returned again. The function must be deterministic: run twice on the same data, it must return the same labels. Fix any random seed or random initialization inside the function, as below. 3.1 Partitioning around medoids library(cluster) set.seed(123) X <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2), matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2) + 4, matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2) - 4) cl_fun <- function(x) cluster::pam(x, k = 3, cluster.only = TRUE) cl <- cl_fun(X) table(cl) #> cl #> 1 2 3 #> 50 50 50 selective_hotelling_bc(X, cl_fun, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, M = 1000)$pval #> [1] 0.0003431453 3.2 A clustering function with a random step If the algorithm uses random numbers, fix the seed inside the function and restore the caller’s random number stream afterwards: cl_fun_random <- function(x) { old <- .Random.seed on.exit(assign(".Random.seed", old, envir = globalenv())) set.seed(1) kmeans(x, centers = 3, nstart = 5)$cluster } selective_hotelling_bc(X, cl_fun_random, k1 = 1, k2 = 2, M = 1000)$pval #> [1] 0.007543708 The same approach works for community detection on a nearest-neighbor graph, as used for single-cell data, or for any other method. 3.3 What selective_hotelling_bc() returns res <- selective_hotelling_bc(X, cl_fun, k1 = 1, k2 = 3, M = 1000) c(pval = res$pval, T2 = res$T_obs, move_fraction = res$move_frac) #> pval T2 move_fraction #> 4.792621e-04 9.510972e+02 7.510000e-01 move_fraction is the fraction of steps at which the Monte Carlo path moved. Values far below about \(0.3\) suggest that the path barely explores the set of data sets that reproduce the clusters, which lowers power but not validity (Chapter 6).

Chapter 4 Tutorial: the one-dimensional test 4.1 Any clustering algorithm 4.2 A closed form for \(k\)-means 4.3 Which test to use

Chapter 4 Tutorial: the one-dimensional test library(selectiveHotelling) selective_truncated_F() computes a second selective \(p\)-value, \(p_{\mathrm{polar,1d}}\). It holds fixed everything about the tested observations except one angle, the one that determines Hotelling’s \(T^2\). Its reference distribution is then a truncated \(F\) distribution in one dimension, which makes it faster to compute. The price is power: fixing more of the data leaves less room to detect a difference (Chapter 6). set.seed(123) X <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2), matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2) + 3, matrix(rnorm(100), ncol = 2) - 3) init <- c(1, 51, 101) cl_fun <- function(x) kmeans_with_fixed_init(x, init_centers_idx = init)$cluster cl <- cl_fun(X) 4.1 Any clustering algorithm With clustering = "custom", the test takes the same clustering function as selective_hotelling_bc() and computes the \(p\)-value by a Monte Carlo path in one dimension: res1d <- selective_truncated_F(X, 1, 2, clustering = "custom", method = "bc", cl_fun = cl_fun, cl_obs = cl, M = 1000) c(onedim = res1d$pval, classical_F = res1d$p_uncond) #> onedim classical_F #> 0.02469193 0.00000000 p_uncond is the classical \(F\) \(p\)-value, which ignores the clustering. 4.2 A closed form for \(k\)-means For \(k\)-means, the \(p\)-value can be computed exactly, without Monte Carlo, if we also condition on the whole sequence of assignments made by Lloyd’s algorithm: res_exact <- selective_truncated_F(X, 1, 2, clustering = "kmeans", method = "exact", K = 3, init_centers_idx = init) res_exact$pval #> [1] 0.04102747 This version conditions on the most, and it is the least powerful of the three tests. 4.3 Which test to use Test Function Conditions on Speed Power \(p_{\mathrm{polar}}\) selective_hotelling_test(), selective_hotelling_bc() the clustering slowest highest \(p_{\mathrm{polar,1d}}\) selective_truncated_F(method = "bc") the clustering and all but one angle faster lower \(p_{\mathrm{polar,1d}}^{\mathrm{traj}}\) selective_truncated_F(method = "exact") also the \(k\)-means trajectory instant lowest All three control the selective Type I error. We recommend \(p_{\mathrm{polar}}\) unless computing time is a constraint.

Chapter 5 Real data: Palmer penguins

Chapter 5 Real data: Palmer penguins library(selectiveHotelling) library(palmerpenguins) The Palmer penguins data contain four body measurements for penguins of three species. We standardize the measurements, cluster the penguins with \(k\)-means, and test every pair of clusters. peng <- na.omit(penguins[, c("species", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g")]) X <- scale(as.matrix(peng[, -1])) species <- peng$species dim(X) #> [1] 342 4 set.seed(1) init <- sample.int(nrow(X), 3) cl_fun <- function(x) kmeans_with_fixed_init(x, init_centers_idx = init)$cluster cl <- cl_fun(X) table(cluster = cl, species) #> species #> cluster Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo #> 1 7 63 0 #> 2 0 0 123 #> 3 144 5 0 naive_pval <- function(X, cl, k1, k2) { n1 <- sum(cl == k1); n2 <- sum(cl == k2); p <- ncol(X); r <- n1 + n2 F_stat <- (r - p - 1) / ((r - 2) * p) * hotelling_T2(X, cl, k1, k2) pf(F_stat, p, r - p - 1, lower.tail = FALSE) } pairs <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(1, 3), c(2, 3)) out <- t(apply(pairs, 1, function(k) { set.seed(10 * k[1] + k[2]) c(k1 = k[1], k2 = k[2], naive = naive_pval(X, cl, k[1], k[2]), selective = selective_hotelling_bc(X, cl_fun, k[1], k[2], M = 1000)$pval) })) signif(out, 3) #> k1 k2 naive selective #> [1,] 1 2 5.08e-117 0.00091 #> [2,] 1 3 4.27e-68 0.20800 #> [3,] 2 3 1.03e-167 0.00837 The clusters match the species: cluster 1 is mostly Chinstrap, cluster 2 is Gentoo, and cluster 3 is mostly Adelie. The naive test rejects every null hypothesis with a vanishingly small \(p\)-value. The selective test rejects the two contrasts that involve the Gentoo cluster, the species that differs most in these measurements, but not the contrast between the Chinstrap and Adelie clusters.

Chapter 6 Technical details and practical advice 6.1 What the tests condition on 6.2 How the \(p\)-value is computed 6.3 Choosing M and L 6.4 Requirements and limitations References

Chapter 6 Technical details and practical advice 6.1 What the tests condition on Write \(\hat{\mathcal C}_1\) and \(\hat{\mathcal C}_2\) for the two tested clusters and \(r = |\hat{\mathcal C}_1| + |\hat{\mathcal C}_2|\). The tests assume that the rows of the data are independent Gaussian vectors with a common covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\), and they test the null hypothesis that all \(r\) observations in the two clusters share one mean. The deviations of the tested observations from their common mean form an \(r \times p\) matrix. Its polar decomposition writes it as \(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{H}\), where \(\mathbf{H}\) is the square root of \(r - 1\) times their sample covariance matrix and \(\mathbf{Q}\) has orthonormal columns. Under the null hypothesis, \(\mathbf{Q}\) is uniformly distributed and independent of \(\mathbf{H}\) and of the rest of the data, whatever \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) is. Hotelling’s \(T^2\) is a function of \(\mathbf{Q}\) alone. So, after fixing \(\mathbf{H}\) and the rest of the data, the only thing left random is \(\mathbf{Q}\), whose distribution is known, and the selective \(p\)-value is the fraction of the matrices \(\mathbf{Q}\) that reproduce the clusters and give a larger \(T^2\) than the observed one. 6.2 How the \(p\)-value is computed The set of matrices \(\mathbf{Q}\) that reproduce the clusters has no closed form. The package walks through it with a Markov chain: each step rotates two rows of \(\mathbf{Q}\) by a random angle, reruns the clustering, and keeps the rotation only if the tested clusters are returned again. The observed \(\mathbf{Q}\) is placed at a random position on a path of M + 1 points, and the \(p\)-value is its rank among them [@BesagClifford1989]. This \(p\)-value is exact for any path length M and any number of steps L between points: a short path gives a valid test with less power. 6.3 Choosing M and L The defaults, M = 5000 and L = 2, are what we use in the paper. Smaller M keeps the test valid but lowers power. M = 1000 is enough for exploration. The clustering is rerun L times at each of the M steps, so the computing time is roughly M * L runs of the clustering algorithm. M and L must be chosen before looking at the data; they must not be tuned on the observed clusters. 6.4 Requirements and limitations Gaussian rows. The guarantee assumes Gaussian data. Heavy tails (for example, \(t\) distributions) can inflate the Type I error, especially after average-linkage hierarchical clustering. Enough observations. The test needs \(r \ge p + 2\), as Hotelling’s \(T^2\) does. For high-dimensional data, reduce the dimension first, for example with principal components computed from data that are not tested. A deterministic clustering function. cl_fun must return the same labels each time it is run on the same data (Chapter 3). The pair to test. The pair should be fixed in advance, or every pair should be tested. Choosing the pair by looking at the data, for example the two clusters that look most different, needs further adjustment. Large clusters. When the two clusters contain hundreds of observations, each step rotates only two of the \(r - 1\) coordinates, and a path of fixed length moves less; the test stays valid but can lose power.
